title: The Meal Chant, The Three Wheels
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of cultivating an attitude of emptiness and interconnectedness in our daily lives, where everything is seen as a gift and not something that can be owned or controlled. This perspective allows us to practice giving and receiving without boundaries, recognizing that all life is always giving and receiving at the same time. By embracing this spirit, we can develop compassion and wisdom in our interactions with others, leading to a deeper understanding of reality and our place within it.

sentences.text: Good morning.
I appreciate that on a beautiful day like this, you did show up for zazen and for the talk.
Tim, are you recording this?
I love summer, the quality of the early light, the warmth of the day.
To me, this is quite wonderful.
But I so appreciate this time together.
It really makes my heart warm.
Last month's Dharma talk was on the five contemplations of the meal chant.
Today I will speak a little bit more about the meal chant.
Tim challenged me yesterday on the three wheels, so that's what we'll talk about: the emptiness of the three wheels, giver, receiver, and gift.
I will apologize upfront that the path to that portion of the meal chant will be quite long today.
I'm a very slow writer in general when it comes to Dharma talks, and this one was slower than most.
The radical interconnectedness of everything is presented in one simple phrase.
And I again confess that I sidetracked myself quite a bit while writing.
There were many interesting detours, fascinating dead ends, and a bridge to nowhere.
There's a lot to unpack.
The three wheels of giver, receiver, and gift very much tie into our studies of the six paramitas, or perfections, that define the Mahayana path.
To recap, the six paramitas are giving, ethical conduct, energy, patience, meditation, and wisdom.
It is often said that there is no hierarchy among the perfections.
But the more I study giving, the more I wonder if it is not the underpinning for all the others.
Maybe giving and the emptiness of the three wheels even is the whole of the Buddha way.
To prepare the ground for our own investigation of the three wheels, let us hear what Dogen wrote about eating.
If you want to read more about that, take a look at the pure standards for the Zen community.
That was one of the sidetracks.
This is from a Dharma talk Dogen gave at Ehichi in 1246.
The name of the talk was Fushuku Hanpo, How to Use Your Bowls.
It begins like this:
*A sutra says, when we are intimate with the food we eat, there is intimacy with all things.
When we are intimate with all things, we are intimate with the food we eat.
We should let all things and eating be intimate with each other, because when each thing is reality, then eating is also reality.
When all things are suchness, then eating is also suchness.
When all things are one awareness, then eating is also one awareness.

When all things are awakened intelligence, then eating is also awakened intelligence. [unclear: "There is any name that can be applied to it"], and the realities spoken of are this intimacy, so we can call of this intimately single.*
Let us keep Dogen's words, this one awareness, and eating as suchness, in mind as I read the first part of the meal chant.
We always chant before we eat during sesshin.
If you know it, feel free to chant along.
*Buddha was born in Kapitalavastu, enlightened in Magadha, taught in Varanasi, entered nirvana in Kushinagara.
Now we set out Buddha's bowls, may we with all beings realize the emptiness of the three wheels, giver, receiver, and gift.

In the midst of the three treasures, which verify our understanding, entrusting ourselves to the sangha, we invoke, Virochana Buddha, pure Dhammakaya, Lohchana Buddha, complete Sambhogakaya, Shakyamuni Buddha, myriad Nimanakaya, Maitreya Buddha of future birth, all Buddhas throughout space and time, Lotus of the wondrous Dharma, Mahayana Sutra, Manjushri Bodhisattva, great wisdom, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, great activity, Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, great compassion, all-honored ones, Bodhisattva, mahasattvas, wisdom beyond wisdom, maha prajnaparamita.*
Our meals during sesshin happen in the context of seated meditation, zazen, lots of zazen.

And of course, as soon as we sit down, thoughts come up, feelings, [unclear: "my need tweaks"], emotions, wants, aversions, thoughts of the past, plans for the future, my ear itches, what-if scenarios, I need to get gas on the way home, what's for lunch?
These thoughts just come up.
I don't know about you, but when I started my meditation practice, I was absolutely certain that the goal of zazen was to have absolutely no thoughts at all for 30 minutes.
Well, [unclear: "when I said thoughts and memories to come up"], but what is the difference that zazen makes?
In the midst of zazen, I am aware of the thought arising.
I bear witness to it and I let it fall away without getting caught, without becoming entangled, without playing the duality games of right and wrong.
No fixing, choosing, or doing needs to take place.
Instead, we return to the breath and let zazen sit itself.
Sometimes a thought hook floats by with the perfect bait and without noticing I get carried away and I am caught.
Then I notice that instead of counting my breath or following my breath or whatever my intention was for this period of zazen, I am planning a trip while I'm trying to figure something out.
And I notice that the older I get, the more time I'm spending trying to figure things out.
But during zazen, a whole different new process happens when we allow the space of the heart.
This is not an escape from life, but a coming home.
If we stay with practice long enough, zazen will take us to the place where we find I am alive and see the same aliveness in everybody else.
We honor it.
It is surprisingly difficult for me to find language to express this.
The foundation, the grounding, the experience of life is in the living itself.
The wide open space in the heart, which is inhabited by life itself, was not shaped by concept or knowledge I acquired.
It was shaped on the cushion, in the chair, by feet touching the floor during kinhin.
It is an understanding that grew over years, excruciatingly slow most of the time.
It is the waking up to life and waking up to my place in it.
Part of the waking up to myself is this: life is a shared experience.
I cannot live by myself.
I cannot survive alone.
We may think that we do all right for ourselves, that we have our credit cards and debit cards, that we are quite independent and don't need anybody else.
So true.
On the other hand, all that didn't help you much when you were in pursuit of a roll of toilet paper and some hand sanitizer when the coronavirus struck.
All the credit cards don't help you when the shelves are empty.
They don't help when the store is closed.
They don't help when people can't come to work.
We do need each other.
I do hope not in a needy way.
We cannot live without each other.
The oxygen I inhale with each breath was produced by plants.
It takes about eight trees to supply enough oxygen for a human being.
Everything I eat comes from a plant or an animal.
This breath I just took, I did nothing to earn it.
It is a gift.
I usually don't say thank you to trees as I pass, though sometimes I do.
This is the oxygen cycle.
Most life on Earth depends on it.
Plants, algae, and some types of bacteria receive energy from sunlight and use it to change carbon dioxide and water to produce oxygen and carbohydrates.
An easy way to understand this cycle is to think that trees breathe in the carbon dioxide and exhale oxygen.
So the tree needs our exhalation too, and sunlight.
The tree is also given a gift.
And the tree needs microbes and soil.
I now know we cannot make it alone.
We are tied into so many webs to receive food and water and air and love.
To live in a house, to drive a car on the road.
We are utterly interdependent.
And with this, I have finally arrived at the part of the meal chant I want to bring up today.
*May we, with all beings, realize the emptiness of the three wheels, giver, receiver, and gift.*
*May we, with all beings, realize the emptiness of the three wheels, giver, receiver, and gift.*
Before we take a look at what these words might mean to us, a few words about emptiness.
In everyday language, a feeling of emptiness isn't anything positive.
It usually means to be devoid of feeling, something missing.
In Zen, on the other hand, it means that nothing we see or hear or are stands alone.
Everything is a tentative expression of a seamless, ever-changing scene.
No person, no individual, no thing has a permanent, fixed identity.
So we are empty of a fixed, separate self, which also means that we are empty of the burden of the self, and empty of boundaries.
Everything taken together is us.
This kind of emptiness, as it is lived and acted by a person of wisdom, comes with its sense of connection, compassion, and love.
In Zen, zazen is just feeling life.
We go deeper and in a different way than we usually do.
There is no better practice than zazen to get in touch with what is really going on.
It is not a cognitive process.
It doesn't work by thought or will.
It's not that we ignore thought or will.
It just doesn't get to run the show this time.
Nevertheless, a lot of processing goes on, even though we don't grab at it, we don't hold on to it, and we don't reject it.
Sitting down, returning awareness to body and breath, and returning the mind to this present moment of being alive.
This attitude is the background of our meal chant.
The emptiness of the three wheels reminds us that the food is a gift.
It has not been earned.
It is a gift from emptiness.
My teacher, Norman Fischer, said this about the three wheels:
*But this gift is not to be understood in the usual way.
The emptiness of the three wheels means that this giving isn't a beneficent act one performs for another, an act you can take credit for or feel worthy or unworthy of.
A Zen practitioner about to eat a meal remembers that giving is life, that everything is giving, everything is given.
There are no separate givers, receivers, or gifts.
All of life is always giving and receiving at the same time.
This is our practice and our joy.
So we practice giving, both receiving and giving gifts, in this spirit.*
End quote.
Another poet, Mary Oliver, says it like this:
*And therefore I look upon everything as a brotherhood and a sisterhood.
And I look upon time as no more than an idea.
And I consider eternity as another possibility.
And I think of each life as a flower, as common as a field daisy and as singular.
And each name a comfortable music in the mouth, tending, as all music does, towards silence.
And each body a line of courage and something precious to the earth.
When it's over, I want to say all my life I was a bride married to amazement.
I was the bridegroom taking the world into my arms.*
This is a part of the poem "When Death Comes."
Early Buddhist literature often mentioned three things we can give: material gifts, the gift of Dharma, and the gift of freedom.
But really, we are not limited.
There are many more things to give.
The gift of listening, the gift of love, the gift of creation, attention, effort, and presence.
To make a poem or a painting is to practice giving.
As is cooking a meal, cleaning a room, putting a flower in a vase, giving a Dharma talk, and listening to it.
Dogen writes that to launch a boat or to build a bridge are acts of giving.
To earn a living, to go to your job, is an act of giving.
To be willing to be born and to die is to practice giving.
I would like to end my talk with a plea.
We live in pretty crazy times.
COVID-19 worldwide has now sickened 18 million people and killed about 700,000.
In the U.S. alone, the numbers stand at four and three quarters of a million who got sick and 158,000 who died.
Many people are unemployed.
Many kids go to bed hungry.
So if you have a neighbor in need, please share.
And if you can give some money to the food bank, please do it.
Because once we see beyond self-absorption, in the field far beyond form and emptiness, in the field of compassion, the three wheels roll on and on.
*Let intention secretly extend to every being and place.
The true merit of Buddha's way.
Beings are numberless.
I vow to save them.
Illusions are inexhaustible.
I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless.
I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable.
I vow to become it.*
